vibeCoding.definition: A development approach where AI agents handle most coding tasks while you provide guidance, make decisions, and verify the results. Think of it as pair programming with AI!
vibeCoding.example: Instead of memorizing syntax, you describe what you want and AI writes the code for you.

react.definition: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces. It lets you create reusable components that update efficiently when your data changes.
react.example: React powers apps like Facebook, Instagram, and Netflix.

vite.definition: A tool that runs a local development server and builds browser files from source. Follow its actual preview URL; the port can change.
vite.example: When you save a file, Vite shows your changes almost immediately.

typescript.definition: JavaScript with type checks that catch some mistakes before running code. It does not replace browser tests or runtime input validation.
typescript.example: TypeScript knows if you're trying to use a number as text and warns you.

api.definition: Application Programming Interface - a way for different software programs to talk to each other. Like a menu at a restaurant: you order from the menu, and the kitchen makes it.
api.example: When you check weather on your phone, it uses an API to get data from a weather service.

restApi.definition: A common style of API that uses HTTP requests (like your web browser uses) to get, create, update, or delete data.
restApi.example: GET /products fetches product data, POST /orders creates a new order.

microsoftGraph.definition: Microsoft's API that lets you access data from Microsoft 365 services like Teams, Outlook, OneDrive, and Azure Active Directory.
microsoftGraph.example: Use Graph API to show a user's calendar or recent emails in your app.

azure.definition: Microsoft's cloud computing platform. Think of it as renting powerful computers and services from Microsoft instead of buying and maintaining your own.
azure.example: An approved deployment can host a website; who can access it depends on its configuration. Cloud use needs a separate cost and permissions review.

tenant.definition: In Microsoft 365/Azure, a tenant is your organization's instance. It's like your company's private section of Microsoft's cloud.
tenant.example: When you sign in with your work email, you're accessing your company's tenant.

msal.definition: Microsoft Authentication Library - code that handles signing users in with their Microsoft accounts and getting permission to access their data.
msal.example: MSAL shows the 'Sign in with Microsoft' button and handles the login process.

environmentVariables.definition: Configuration supplied to a program. Environment variables are not automatically secret: VITE_ values can be included in browser-delivered files.
environmentVariables.example: VITE_APP_NAME may hold a public title. Never put passwords or API keys in VITE_ variables, even in an ignored .env.local file.

npm.definition: The package manager and script runner included with Node.js. It downloads reusable code and runs commands defined by a project's package.json. Packages can run code during installation, so review what you install.
npm.example: 'npm install react' downloads React so you can use it in your project.

nodejs.definition: A program that lets you run JavaScript on your computer (not just in a browser). Many web dev tools (like Vite) use Node.js.
nodejs.example: When you run 'npm install' or 'npm run dev', you're using Node.js under the hood.

lts.definition: Long-Term Support: a release support policy used by some projects. Not every library has an LTS release.
lts.example: This lab uses Node.js 24 LTS. Choose compatible stable React and Vite packages and preserve their resolved versions in the lockfile.

git.definition: Version control system that tracks every change to your code. Like 'Track Changes' in Word, but way more powerful.
git.example: If you break something, Git lets you go back to a working version.

repo.definition: Short for repository — a project folder that Git tracks. A repo usually contains your code plus files like package.json and README.md.
repo.example: A GitHub repo can be cloned to your computer so you can edit the code.

fork.definition: A copy of someone else's GitHub repo under your own account. You fork when you want your own version you can push changes to.
fork.example: Fork a starter kit repo, then make changes in your fork without affecting the original.

clone.definition: Make a local copy of a Git repository and its history. Add the folder as a local project in the Copilot desktop app if you want to work on it there.
clone.example: 'git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git' creates a local folder with the project.

vscode.definition: Visual Studio Code is a separate code editor. This course uses the GitHub Copilot desktop app instead; VS Code is not required.
vscode.example: An instruction to open a VS Code extension is not an instruction for the Copilot desktop app.

instructionFiles.definition: Special .md files that tell GitHub Copilot how to behave in your project (coding standards, tech choices, accessibility rules, etc.). They help keep the AI consistent.
instructionFiles.example: A React instruction file might require TypeScript strict mode and accessible components.

mcpServers.definition: External tools connected to an AI client through Model Context Protocol. They may expose data or actions and need a permissions review. Not required for the beginner lab.
mcpServers.example: A documentation tool can return references; a connected tool does not guarantee generated code is correct.

context7.definition: An MCP server that gives Copilot up-to-date library documentation and code examples. Useful when you want current APIs instead of outdated guesses.
context7.example: Ask Copilot to check Context7 for the latest React Router patterns.

playwright.definition: A tool for automated browser testing. It can click buttons, fill forms, and verify what a user would see in Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
playwright.example: Run Playwright tests to confirm your app works after a change.

beastMode.definition: A name used for custom agent instructions, not a built-in guarantee of quality, security, or production readiness. It is not required for this lab.
beastMode.example: Use the desktop app's normal local session and verify each small change instead of installing a custom agent.

planMode.definition: An approach where Copilot proposes work for review before implementation. Ask for a small plan with observable checks; app mode labels can vary by build.
planMode.example: Plan one record type and four small increments. Do not create files until the plan is approved.

component.definition: A reusable piece of UI in React. Like LEGO blocks - you build your app by combining components.
component.example: A Button component can be reused throughout your app with different labels and colors.

props.definition: Short for 'properties' - data you pass into a React component. Like function parameters, but for UI.
props.example: <Button color='blue' label='Click me' /> passes color and label as props.

state.definition: Data that can change over time in your React component. When state changes, React re-renders the UI automatically.
state.example: A counter's current value is state - click a button, state updates, UI updates.

hook.definition: Special React functions that let you use features like state and lifecycle methods. They start with 'use'.
hook.example: useState, useEffect, useContext are all hooks.

tailwind.definition: A tool that helps you style your app by adding small class names right in your HTML/JSX (instead of writing lots of separate CSS files).
tailwind.example: A class like 'p-4' adds padding and 'text-white' makes text white.

jsx.definition: JavaScript XML - a syntax that lets you write HTML-like code in JavaScript. React's secret sauce!
jsx.example: const button = <button>Click me</button> looks like HTML but it's JavaScript.

deployment.definition: The process of putting your app on the internet so others can use it. Like publishing a book, but for software.
deployment.example: Deploy to Azure Static Web Apps to get a public URL for your app.

cicd.definition: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment - automatically testing and deploying your code when you make changes.
cicd.example: Push code to GitHub, tests run automatically, if they pass, deploy to production.

dataverse.definition: Microsoft's cloud database designed for Power Platform apps. Stores your business data with built-in security and relationships.
dataverse.example: Store customer records, orders, and products in Dataverse tables.

pcf.definition: PowerApps Component Framework - lets you create custom controls for Power Apps using React, Angular, or vanilla JavaScript.
pcf.example: Build a fancy chart component in React and use it in your Power App.

powerApps.definition: Microsoft's low-code/no-code platform for building business apps. Now you can add custom code components too!
powerApps.example: Build an expense approval app without traditional coding (or enhance it with code components).

modelDrivenApp.definition: A type of Power App that automatically generates UI based on your data model. Great for complex business apps.
modelDrivenApp.example: Define customer and order tables, Power Apps creates forms and views automatically.

canvasApp.definition: A type of Power App where you design the UI pixel-by-pixel. Maximum flexibility and creativity.
canvasApp.example: Drag and drop buttons, forms, and galleries to design your app's exact look.

solution.definition: In Power Platform, a container for all your components (apps, tables, flows) that you can move between environments.
solution.example: Build in dev environment, export solution, import to production.

customPage.definition: A full-screen page in model-driven apps where you can use React and custom code. Perfect for embedding Code Components!
customPage.example: Add a custom dashboard page with interactive charts to your model-driven app.

pacCli.definition: Power Platform CLI - command-line tools for developing, testing, and deploying Power Platform components.
pacCli.example: pac pcf init creates a new Code Component project.

csp.definition: Content Security Policy. A browser security feature that controls which scripts, styles, images, and network requests your app is allowed to load. It helps protect users from attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS).
csp.example: If a page refuses to load a script/style from a domain, CSP is often the reason.

eslint.definition: A code linter for JavaScript/TypeScript that finds common bugs and style issues while you code. It helps keep code consistent and catches problems early.
eslint.example: ESLint can warn when you forget to handle a promise or when a variable is never used.

prettier.definition: An automatic code formatter. It reformats your code into a consistent style so you don’t spend time arguing about spacing, quotes, or line breaks.
prettier.example: Format-on-save makes files look consistent across a team.

azureStaticWebApps.definition: A hosting service for static front-end apps (and optional APIs) that integrates with GitHub for automatic builds and deployments.
azureStaticWebApps.example: Push to GitHub, and Azure Static Web Apps builds your Vite app and deploys it to a public URL.

githubPages.definition: Free static hosting from a GitHub repository. Great for demos, docs, and simple front-end apps.
githubPages.example: Deploy your built site so it’s available at https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/.

crud.definition: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations most apps perform on data.
crud.example: A products screen usually supports CRUD: add a product, view it, edit it, and delete it.

authentication.example: Signing in with Microsoft, Google, or email/password.

authorization.definition: Determining what an authenticated user is allowed to do (permissions).
authorization.example: Admins can delete records; viewers can only read.

rbac.definition: A common authorization approach where permissions come from roles (Admin, Manager, Viewer, etc.).
rbac.example: If your role is Viewer, the Delete button is hidden and the API blocks deletes.

sql.definition: Structured Query Language — the standard language used to query and manage relational databases.

firebase.definition: A Google platform for building apps quickly, including hosted databases, authentication, storage, and hosting.
firebase.example: Use Firebase Auth for login and Firestore to store app data.

pwa.definition: Progressive Web App — a website that can behave more like an app (installable icon, offline support, caching, etc.).
pwa.example: Your app can load even when the network is flaky, using cached assets.

unitTests.definition: Tests that verify small pieces of code (functions/components) in isolation.
unitTests.example: A unit test checks that a validator rejects an invalid email.

integrationTests.definition: Tests that verify multiple pieces work together (components + data + APIs), usually with some real wiring.
integrationTests.example: Render a page, click Save, and verify the API call and UI state update.

e2e.definition: End-to-end testing — tests that drive the app like a real user (browser automation).
e2e.example: Open the app, log in, create a record, and verify it shows up in the list.

pdfLib.definition: A JavaScript library for creating and editing PDF files in the browser or Node.js.
pdfLib.example: Generate an invoice PDF and let the user download it.

jspdf.definition: A popular library for generating PDFs in the browser.
jspdf.example: Export a receipt or simple report as a PDF.

reactPdfRenderer.definition: A React-based way to generate PDFs using React components and styling.
reactPdfRenderer.example: Build a PDF document using React components like <Text> and <View>.

docxPkg.definition: A library for creating .docx Word documents using TypeScript/JavaScript.
docxPkg.example: Generate a compliance letter or summary document.

docxtemplater.definition: A library for filling Word document templates (.docx) with data.
docxtemplater.example: Create a template with placeholders like {name} and fill it from form data.

three.definition: Three.js — a 3D graphics library for the web.
three.example: Render a 3D product viewer in your app.

reactThreeFiber.definition: A React renderer for Three.js, letting you build 3D scenes using React components.
reactThreeFiber.example: Use React components to compose lights, meshes, and cameras.

reactThreeDrei.definition: A helper library with useful components and utilities for @react-three/fiber.
reactThreeDrei.example: Drop in orbit controls, loaders, and ready-made primitives.

recharts.definition: A charting library built for React, with composable chart components.
recharts.example: Add a sales trend line chart or a category pie chart.

chartjs.definition: A widely used JavaScript charting library.
chartjs.example: Render bar charts, line charts, and doughnut charts.

tanstackReactTable.definition: A headless table library for building powerful data tables in React.
tanstackReactTable.example: Sortable columns, pagination, filtering, and row selection.

reactHookForm.definition: A popular React library for building forms with good performance and great ergonomics.
reactHookForm.example: Handle validation, errors, and form state with minimal re-renders.

zod.definition: A TypeScript-first schema validation library. It validates data at runtime and can infer TypeScript types from schemas.
zod.example: Validate a form payload and show friendly errors when something is missing or invalid.

tanstackReactQuery.definition: A library for data fetching, caching, retries, and managing server state in React.
tanstackReactQuery.example: Fetch a list of items, cache it, and automatically refetch when it becomes stale.

zustand.definition: A small, fast state management library for React.
zustand.example: Store global UI state like theme, filters, or user preferences.

copilotDesktop.definition: The desktop AI coding app used in this course for local project sessions, prompts, and change review. It is not GitHub Desktop, Copilot CLI, or the VS Code extension.
copilotDesktop.example: Install from GitHub's official download page, sign in, and verify a chat reply before starting the lab.

github.definition: A website for hosting code and collaborating. Git is the local history tool; GitHub is an online service. A GitHub account is also used to sign in to Copilot.
github.example: You can save a local Git commit without uploading your app to GitHub.

branch.definition: A named line of work in Git. It lets you keep one set of changes separate from another until you choose to combine them.
branch.example: Record the branch name with your commit ID so you can return to the same work.

markdown.definition: Plain text with simple formatting markers. A # starts a heading, and a dash starts a list item. Markdown files usually end in .md.
markdown.example: A SKILL.md file describes a reusable task for Copilot. The filename must not end in .md.txt.

json.definition: A text format for structured settings or data. Names and text values use double quotes; commas separate entries. Ordinary JSON does not allow comments or trailing commas.
json.example: An MCP configuration contains a server name, connection type, and address. Preserve existing entries when adding one.

skills.definition: Reusable task instructions in a folder containing SKILL.md. Copilot can load a relevant skill when needed. A skill is not a new model, a permission grant, or proof that its advice is correct.
skills.example: A locally written review skill asks for expected versus actual test results and labels unrun checks as NOT RUN.

terminal.definition: A text window that runs commands on your computer. It is different from Copilot chat and your web browser. In these labs, Copilot runs the commands for you and shows the output.
terminal.example: Ask Copilot to run node --version; it runs the command in its terminal and shows you the result.

prompt.definition: A request you send to an AI assistant in chat. A useful prompt says what you want, what must not change, and how you will check the result.
prompt.example: Ask for one labeled Name field, then try both a real name and a blank name.

workspace.definition: The folder where a session reads files and runs commands. A terminal's working directory is the folder it currently uses. Check it before changing anything.
workspace.example: Your learner app and this learning portal must be in different folders.

dependency.definition: A reusable code package needed by an app or its development tools. Installing dependencies downloads other people's code; use approved sources.
dependency.example: npm install downloads the packages listed in package.json.

localhost.definition: An address meaning this computer. A localhost preview is not a public website and will not show your app on someone else's computer.
localhost.example: Open the exact Local URL printed by Vite on the computer running the app.

session.definition: A conversation and working context in the Copilot desktop app. The beginner lab uses a local session.
session.example: Keep one session for the learner app and check its actual working directory before running commands.

worktree.definition: A separate checkout of a Git repository. A desktop session may work here instead of in the original project folder.
worktree.example: Use the session's actual path for commands and reviews. Preserve its work before removing the session.

scaffold.definition: The smallest set of files and settings needed to run an app.
scaffold.example: Create one page with two sample records, preview it, and only then add a form.

acceptanceCriteria.definition: Observable results you use to decide whether a feature works. A claim from the AI is not the same as checking the result yourself.
acceptanceCriteria.example: Submitting a spaces-only name shows an error and does not add a record.

syntheticData.definition: Completely made-up data used for practice, not copied from people or business systems.
syntheticData.example: Demo clipboard request is a fictional supply request, not a patient record.

localStorage.definition: Browser storage that can keep records after refresh for one profile and origin. It can be cleared and is not secure storage, cross-device sync, or backup.
localStorage.example: A changed port or another browser can show a separate set of records.

origin.definition: The scheme, host, and port of a website address. Browser storage is separated by origin.
origin.example: http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:5174 use different storage.

lockfile.definition: A file that records resolved package versions. Keep package-lock.json to reproduce an npm dependency tree.
lockfile.example: npm ci restores the recorded dependencies without choosing a new dependency tree.

diff.definition: A view of added and removed content. Review it before accepting or committing changes; inspect new files too.
diff.example: Confirm a form fix did not remove validation or change unrelated files.

commit.definition: A saved snapshot in local Git history. A commit does not push, publish, deploy, or create an off-device backup.
commit.example: After reviewing the staged files, save a local checkpoint and record its ID.

exitCode.definition: A number returned by a finished command. Usually 0 means success and a nonzero number means failure.
exitCode.example: Record exit code 0 for both npm run build and npm run lint, after reading their output.

pullRequest.definition: A GitHub page that proposes merging one branch into another. People, AI reviewers, and automated checks can comment before anyone merges.
pullRequest.example: Open a pull request for the rename feature, wait for checks to pass, read the review, then decide whether to merge.

autopilot.definition: A Copilot app session mode where the agent writes code, runs commands, and iterates without waiting for you between steps. You still review the result.
autopilot.example: Use Autopilot only after you have passing tests, a written spec, a saved commit, and clear stop conditions.

sandbox.definition: A restricted place to run commands. A local sandbox limits which files, networks, and credentials agent-run tools can reach; a cloud sandbox runs the whole session on GitHub's computers.
sandbox.example: Type /sandbox on in a local session before letting the agent work more independently.

customAgent.definition: A Markdown agent profile that gives Copilot a focused role, its own instructions, and optionally a limited set of tools.
customAgent.example: A test-reviewer agent with only read and search tools can review tests but cannot edit files.

contextWindow.definition: The limited amount of text an AI model can consider at once, including your messages, attached files, tool output, and its own replies.
contextWindow.example: Type /context to see how full the session is. Attach the one file that matters instead of the whole project.

spec.definition: Short for specification: a written description of what a feature must do, what it must not do, and how you will check it.
spec.example: A rename spec lists the name rules, the keyboard behavior, and three checks you can run in the browser.

regression.definition: Something that used to work and is now broken, usually because of a recent change.
regression.example: If adding rename made the Add form accept blank names again, that would be a regression. A saved test catches it.
